intro: Three BC techniques, seen before they are drilled. Parts turns $\int u\,dv$ into $uv - \int v\,du$: the picture shows why, as two areas that fill a rectangle. Partial fractions split a rational function into simple pieces you can integrate one at a time. An improper integral is the limit of ordinary ones: stretch the bound and watch the area settle on a number or grow forever. Then Test yourself, including a drill on choosing the method.
howItWorks:
Parts. Name $u$ (the factor that gets simpler when differentiated: logarithms, then powers of $x$) and $dv$ (the factor you can integrate), find $du$ and $v$, and write $uv - \int v\,du$. For $x^2$ times $e^{ax}$, $\sin ax$ or $\cos ax$, the tabular method does the repeated parts in one table: differentiate down one column to 0, integrate down the other, and add the diagonal products with signs $+, -, +$. The picture plots $u$ against $v$: the area under that curve is $\int u\,dv$, the area beside it is $\int v\,du$, and together they make $uv$ at the upper bound minus $uv$ at the lower.

Partial fractions (BC: distinct linear factors only). Write $\frac{N(x)}{(x - a)(x - b)} = \frac{A}{x - a} + \frac{B}{x - b}$ and find $A$ by covering up $x - a$ and putting $x = a$ into what is left; then each piece integrates to a logarithm, $A\ln|x - a|$.

Improper integrals. Replace the infinite bound (or the bound where the integrand blows up) by $b$, integrate, and take the limit as $b$ goes there, with limit notation to the end: no arithmetic with $\infty$. A finite limit means the integral converges to it; otherwise it diverges. $\int_1^{\infty} \frac{1}{x^p}\,dx$ converges exactly when $p > 1$, and $\int_0^1 \frac{1}{x^p}\,dx$ exactly when $p < 1$.

Typed answers are checked by evaluating them, so any correct form counts; an antiderivative needs its $+ C$. A wrong answer gets the name of the slip it matches: the sign in $uv - \int v\,du$, two antiderivatives multiplied, a missing chain factor, all-plus tabular signs, $A$ and $B$ swapped, $\ln$ without absolute values, a limit written with $\infty$ plugged in.
